5809: The whale shark Rhincodon typus is the world’s largest extant species of fish, and aggregates normally to capitalize on foraging opportunities. The species’ predictable occurrence at certain sites globally have made them a considerable attraction for marine wildlife tourism. In Oslob, Philippines, the whale shark tourism operation uses daily feeding to allow tourists to have close, near-shore interactions with the sharks. The sharks have now been visited by 1 million tourists since 2012 -- making Oslob as world’s largest non-captive whale shark tourism destination. Here, we used 8-year longitudinal data of their daily presence in Oslob to assess seasonality, abundance and population dynamics of the aggregation. Through photoidentification, we identified 428 individual whale sharks between March 31, 2012 and December 31, 2019, with 300 males, 82 females, and 44 of unknown sex, with a mean total length of 4.93 ± 1.29 m, consistently juvenile male-biased like most other coastal aggregations globally. Unlike most aggregations globally, the sharks in Oslob occur daily, year-round, with a maximum of 38 individuals seen in a single day, and a minimum of 1. Individual P-403, first identified on June 10, 2012, was the individual that most frequented the site (1,697 out of 2742 days), while 20% of the aggregation were only sighted once. A total of 87 sharks were also resighted in other places in the Philippines, with one matched to Malaysia, highlighting their highly mobile nature. Scars were observed in 35% of the aggregation which emphasizes the need to improve local and national legislation for their protection. Although some extended or year-round occurrence has been documented in places like Tanzania and the Maldives, the predictability in Oslob is unique highlighting the impacts of provisioning activities on this Endangered species. Assessing long-term fluctuations in abundance and behaviour at the individual and population levels are imperative.

5810: The Global Finprint project has spent the last few years carrying out baited remote underwater video stations at more than 370 reefs in 58 nations making it the most comprehensive study of coral reef sharks and rays. The results demonstrate that as a group reef sharks have declined dramatically. At least 20% of reefs surveyed had no reef sharks recorded, and this group is believed to be ecologically extinct in these areas. The use of MPAs, fishing controls and improved governance were demonstrated to provide pathways to improve reef shark status. Using data for individual species, and accounting for coral reef area in the nations surveyed we were able to demonstrate that declines in reef sharks has led to increased extinction risk for species in both the IndoPacific and Atlantic oceans, with most species likely to qualify for Vulnerable or Endangered categories of the IUCN Red List. The response of coral reef ray populations has been more complex with the loss of sharks leading to increases in the abundance of small rays such as mask and lagoon rays in some locations. However, in many locations rays were also not observed. However, these rays may not yet meet criteria for listing in threatened categories of the IUCN Red List. The global Finprint study has provided a unique window into the world of sharks and rays that live on coral reefs, providing evidence of concerning declines but also avenues to achieve conservation success.

5811: Negative shark-human interactions are relatively unpredictable and ungovernable events. These events draw significant media attention and historically have elicited emotionally driven public perceptions of sharks. Governments and communities globally have developed extensive shark safety guidelines intended to minimize public risk with sharks. However, expert workshops and community outreach suggested that communities may not strictly adhere to the advice presented. Scientists and communities alike have also indicated they wish to learn the scientific evidence substantiating such guidelines to inform individual risk assessments. This review assessed the scientific basis of safety guidelines intended to minimise shark bite risk. Current literature on shark ecology and behaviour was compared with 36 shark safety guidelines identified from six global governments with high shark bite incidence. 5816: Anthropogenic inputs have caused atmospheric CO 2 levels to rise at an unprecedented rate and, unless curtailed, are anticipated to drastically increase the global surface and ocean temperatures. 5818: Unique individual markings are observed in numerous species, and have been used to understand their movement ecology and population dynamics. 5821: Age and growth data are central to management or conservation strategies for any species. 5822: The energetics of an animal – its energy requirements and allocation to bodily processes – provides insight into trophodynamics and survival. Forecasting the plasticity of animal responses to environmental change can inform ecosystem and species management. However, the use of energy reserves did not account for all of the costs of reproduction. 5825: Movement of large marine predators can connect remote or isolated habitats, and create links that are key for maintaining connectivity within and between ecosystems. We used a combination of acoustic telemetry data, network analysis, habitat modelling, and machine learning methods to quantify movement patterns and habitat use of three coral reef predators (grey reef shark Carcharhinus amblyrhynchos, silvertip shark Carcharhinus albimarginatus and red bass Lutjanus bohar). Grey reef sharks displayed greater movement than silvertip sharks and red bass, with connectivity linking distant reefs and atolls. Movement patterns and connectivity was more extensive at Rowley Shoals than at Scott Reef. However, all three species preferred habitats with moderate to low structural complexity close to the reef and/or to passages in the reef crest, a pattern that was consistent between the two reef systems. Red bass movements resulted in local-scale connectivity between the lagoon and nearby forereef areas, whereas shark connectivity operated at broader scales creating greater linkages across distant areas within the reef systems. Despite some limitation in sample size we were able to compare movements of reef predators and identify species-specific habitat preferences driving habitat use and connectivity in two reef systems. Importantly, we show that existing spatial planning at these remote coral reefs is effective to protect local-scale movements of mesopredators, but that spatial protection at broader scales is still needed to effectively maintain the connectivity of large predators, which is crucial for the stability of isolated coral reef ecosystems.

5826: An understanding of the vertical movements of elasmobranchs across their range is crucial to defining critical habitat use and its overlap with anthropogenic activities, and subsequently managing such interactions. 5828: Galapagos sharks, Carcharhinus galapagensis, are abundant in the Lord Howe Island Marine Park (LHIMP; covering State and Commonwealth waters) and are a key indicator species for monitoring and management. However, little is known about this species in the LHIMP and there is a pressing need to understand their movement ecology and behaviour because they regularly consume bait and hooked fish (depredation), leading to negative outcomes for fishers (social and economic) and sharks (injury or deliberate killing of sharks by fishers). We present data from an ongoing acoustic telemetry study of Galapagos sharks from January 2018 to January 2020, where 30 juvenile sharks were tagged with acoustic transmitters and charter fishing vessel activity was monitored using Vessel Monitoring System data. Sharks were detected throughout all months of the year, peaking in November, and they moved widely throughout the LHIMP, including crossing a deep-water (>1000 m) channel between the Lord Howe Island shelf and Ball’s Pyramid shelf. Kernel Utilisation Distribution analysis identified shark core use areas ranging from 1.2 - 217.6 km2 (mean ± SD = 50.7 ± 66.3 km2). Tag depth data indicated that sharks ranged from 0 - 95 m, with large variations in vertical movements between individuals. Generalised Additive Mixed Models revealed that shark occupancy at receiver locations (number of detections) was positively influenced by increasing fishing activity. Increasing bathymetric complexity and sea surface temperature also had a positive influence on number of detections. High residency values of up to 0.76 were recorded for three sharks at a location where fish waste is discarded, which may indicate a possible change in the movement patterns of these sharks due to the availability of this food source. This study provides detailed insights into the behaviour and movement ecology of this species and is a critical first step towards informing future research and community-driven management to reduce negative interactions between fishers and sharks in the LHIMP.

5829: Detections of tagged animals in passive acoustic telemetry arrays are primarily determined by the spatial configuration of the receivers. However, maintenance of multiple receivers is expensive, and there is a need to configure acoustic receiver arrays in a way that maximises detection probability while minimising cost. This study utilised data from a dense acoustic receiver array deployed off Port Stephens on the east coast of Australia at a known coastal aggregation site for white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias) to assess how detection data of tagged white sharks in the area was affected by reducing the array size post hoc. Reduced arrays were sampled using three methods: fully random sampling as a base scenario, random sampling from spatially grouped clusters of receivers, and sampling of the top performing receivers. Using the top performing receivers, array size could be reduced by 60% (10 out of 25 receivers) and still reliably detect 100% of white sharks detected with the full array. Even with the random and clustered sampling methods this could be achieved with a 20% reduction in array size (20 out of 25 receivers). Reducing by 60% of the array size using the top performing receivers resulted in only an approximately 30% decrease in the average numbers of detections per visit of the tagged sharks (117 out of 171 detections), while reducing that same amount using the random and clustered sampling methods resulted in an approximately 60% decrease in average numbers of detections (68 and 71 out of 171 detections respectively). Although these results are specific to the Port Stephens array, the top receiver sampling method used in this study presents an experimental method of optimising placement of limited receiver resources that could be applied to design and assess spatial configurations of novel acoustic arrays for monitoring in similar habitats.

5830: Advances in biologging technology have enabled researchers to monitor the fine-scale movements and behaviour of numerous elasmobranchs, improving our understanding of how these animals behave and the biomechanics behind their swimming behaviours. With this said, there is very little information detailing the fine-scale behaviour of Batoids through the use of biologgers. In this study, we used high resolution multi-sensor biologging packages that record tri-axial acceleration, depth, temperature and speed to examine the fine-scale swimming behaviour and activity of the southern eagle ray (Myliobatis tenuicaudatus) in southeast Tasmania, Australia. A total of seven rays (874 ± 158 mm wing length; mean and ± SD) were tagged over two sampling periods: 4 individuals in 2014 and 3 individuals in 2020. Tag attachment time ranged from 68 h 43 m to 94 h 31 m (81 h 15 min ± 11 h 1 min; mean and ± SD) with a total of over 568 h of acceleration data recorded. Eagle rays exploited depths ranging from 0 - 38.18 m, swimming at an overall mean depth of 4.03 ± 4.17 m and experienced mean temperatures between 15.98 and 18.76 °C. All rays oscillated through the water column at relatively shallow angles, descending and ascending at an overall mean angle of -9.72 ± 4.76 ° and 9.32 ± 4.78° respectively. Initial investigations show that during descents, all animals exhibited periods of gliding behaviour. Further analysis will be undertaken to investigate this gliding behaviour to improve our understanding of why this behaviour is employed. Additional analyses will also investigate differences in diel behaviour and the biomechanics employed during swimming, providing the first insights into the fine-scale swimming behaviour and activity of the southern eagle ray and Batoids in general.

5831: The benefits of no-take MPAs, or marine reserves (MRs), for commercially exploited fish have been widely demonstrated, including in NZ, where reef-associated species have benefited from protection. In contrast, the effects of MRs on large and mobile species, such as sharks, are poorly studied in NZ. Given the current pressures facing shark populations, it is important to research the benefits that MRs may provide. Although most coastal MRs in NZ are relatively small, sharks may still benefit indirectly from the recovery of prey populations within protected habitats. This research thus aimed to investigate MRs in southern NZ to determine whether they have affected the distribution of coastal sharks. BRUVs (baited remote underwater video systems) were used to determine the relative abundance of sharks within six MRs and adjacent control sites in Fiordland and Stewart Island. 317 deployments were completed between April 2018 and December 2019. In addition, environmental DNA (eDNA) was integrated into the study during 30 deployments to compare the two techniques for detecting elasmobranchs, as well the efficacy of eDNA for MR monitoring. The main results showed that in Fiordland, mesopredatory sharks appear to be benefiting from protection, as a significant MR effect was observed. In contrast, a negligible MR effect was found for broadnose sevengill sharks. As broadnose sevengill sharks are a mobile top predator with a larger home range than mesopredators, these findings suggest that mesopredators with smaller home ranges are more likely to benefit from MRs in Fiordland. These results, therefore, emphasise the need to consider the size of MRs required for effective protection of species with different ranging behaviour. This study presents the first attempt to assess the effect of MRs on coastal elasmobranchs in NZ and will provide important insights into the applicability of eDNA as a tool for monitoring MRs.
5832: The life span of the Greenland shark is at least 272 years and may be as long as 500 years making this animal the longest living vertebrate on the planet. It was one of the lesser-known species of sharks up until 2016 when its extreme longevity was revealed. The finding that they live in the deep, dark Arctic waters for hundreds of years has captured the imagination of the world and the attention of scientists. How does an animal born in Shakespeare's time still patrol the deep today? This extreme longevity is particularly interesting with respect to the heart, because heart disease is synonymous with aging in humans. What structures do their hearts have that permit this extreme longevity? Does the heart underlie the ability of this shark to live so long? We investigated cardiac tissue from 8 sharks whose ages range between ~ 100±120 to 210 ±120 years old and found significant fibrosis, evidence of cardiomyocyte proliferation and regeneration and unusual mitochondrial biology. We did not find evidence of atherosclerosis. These findings will be discussed in relation to the idea of chronological age versus 'biological' age.

5833: Injection of neural tracers into selected branches of cranial nerves V, VII, IX and X that innervate respiratory muscles and the heart of the elasmobranch fish, Scyliorhinus canicula identified their progressive rostro-caudal distribution into discrete nuclei in the brainstem. Efferent activity recorded from nerves supplying respiratory muscles inserted on the jaws, hyomandibular and gill arches displayed sequential bursting activity, driving gill ventilation. This activity, which may be derive from a respiratory rhythm generator located in the reticular formation, was relayed via the trigeminal Vth nucleus, with subsequent activity in the VIIth, IXth and Xth nuclei reflecting their location in the brainstem. Forced ventilation is achieved by recruitment of feeding muscles, innervated by occipital and anterior spinal nerves. The heart and branchial (gill) circulation in elasmobranch fishes is innervated solely by the parasympathetic vagus nerve. Recordings from cardiac branches of the vagus showed two types of activity: units with regular, respiration-related activity and arrhythmic activity that increased during hypoxia and in response to J-recepter stimulation. Injection of neural tracers into the cardiac nerves revealed that cardiac, vagal, preganglionic neurons (CVPN) have their cell bodies in two locations in the brainstem: medial (m) within the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (DVN) and a ventro-lateral scattered distribution (vl) outside of the DVN. Location of these cell bodies by insertion into the brainstem of recording micro-electrodes revealed that m cells showed respiration-related activity while vl cells did not. Both cell groups responded to mechanical stimulation of gill arches. Although tonic, peripheral electrical stimulation of cardiac branches of the vagus inhibited the heart, phasic stimulation recruited the heart at rates faster or slower than its intrinsic rate. A simple model attempting to explain the nature and significance of some of these interactions has been proposed.

5834: Despite their evolutionary success, many chondrichthyans are increasingly threatened with extinction as a result of human activities and the conservative life history traits of this group of fishes. In Mediterranean basin, the thornback ray (Raja clavata), represents among the Rajids the most commercially utilized species and it is actually included in the IUCN-RedList as Threatened species. In particular, in the West-Central Mediterranean basin, where the fishing activity is well-developed, R. clavata represents one of the most important by-catch species mostly for the bottom trawl and long line fishery. Despite being a very widespread species, some gaps still exist on its biology mostly on the growth pattern. The lack of biological data constitutes, for the Mediterranean, one of the impediments in order to assess and take appropriate management measures for this species. Indeed, stock-assessment models, particularly the analytical ones, require growth parameters as important input data. The aim of the present study is to fill this knowledge gap. Specimens of R. clavata were collected during the experimental trawl surveys, commercial landings and discard monitoring in Sardinia, Central-Southern Tyrrhenian, West Ionian and South Adriatic Sea. Thin sections of vertebrae were performed in order to determinate the age and calculate the von Bertalanffy growth function parameters for both sexes in each study area. Moreover, on specimens captured in Adriatic, Sardinia and West Ionian, the marginal increment analysis (MIA) of the vertebrae was also carried out as a semidirect ageing analysis validation. In the Adriatic, a mark-recapture experiment, marking by both external (spaghetti tags) and chemical (oxytetracycline injection) tags, 98 specimens of R. clavata was also realized. In total two recaptures after 11 and 14 months were recorded with an increment in total length respectively of 11.4 cm (from 49.5 to 60.9 cm) and 10.3 cm (from 63.5 to 73.8 cm). In both specimens recaptured the oxytetracycline mark together with the subsequent deposition of a completed annulus (one transparent and opaque ring) was observed on the sections of vertebrae.

5835: Morphometric characters have traditionally been used to describe fish population structures and differences between populations. They have been found to be of taxonomic importance in sex, race and species identification as well. Knowledge involving the taxonomy, systematics and life history of rays and skates that inhabit the Mediterranean basin is scarce. Up to date the importance of batoids in small-scale fisheries in the Greek waters is not well-known, possibly due to the taxonomic uncertainties concerning several taxa. The aim of this work was to present for the first time the morphometric characters of Raja clavata in the eastern Ionian Sea, in order to identify differences between sexes and compare them to other rajids in future references. Intraspecific variation in the external morphology of the thornback ray was investigated and described on the basis of 35 morphometric variables, from 77 females (140-780 mm in total length) and 63 males (135-690 mm in total length). For each morphometric value the mean, standard deviation, range and coefficient variation (CV) were estimated for each sex separately. Regression models were applied to estimate the relationships between each morphometric character and total length. The pattern of allometry for each parameter was established by testing the slope (b) of the obtained regression equations against isometry applying the Student's t-test. (b = 1 for length-length or 3 for length-weight). The length-weight relationship was determined according to the following equation: W=a*TLb. Differences between sexes were tested with t-test. Further investigation on different sizes of R.clavata will contribute to the knowledge of the stock biology, physiology and ecology.

5836: The body (somatic) growth of individuals is a vital process that governs many aspects of a species' life history. Thus, knowledge about growth parameters is critical in many assessment methods. Such growth parameters are derived by relating individual length to age, with the latter commonly estimated from growth bands formed in calcified structures. Recent research, however, suggests that these structures cannot be used for aging in many elasmobranchs (sharks, rays and skates). Alternative methods from mark-recapture tagging data have been proposed in the past, but have not been rigorously tested on elasmobranchs. Therefore, the performance of seven different methods in estimating von Bertalanffy growth parameters for elasmobranchs is investigated here. The performance of the methods were evaluated in two ways: 1) Estimated growth parameters from simulated datasets that considered individual growth variability, measurement error and different scenarios for the length at capture, times at liberty and sample size were compared to the true growth parameters in the simulation; 2) Growth parameters were estimated from empirical mark-recapture tagging data for 15 different elasmobranch stocks and compared to literature growth parameters obtained from length-at-age information. Best practicies when only limited information from mark-recapture tagging data is available will be presented with practical applications and common pitfalls discussed.

5837: The different effects of fishing capture are not just immediate death; unwanted animals are released back into the environment to an unknown fate, as injuries and physiological, physical and behavioural consequences can ultimately lead to delayed mortality and/or impact their fitness. In teleosts, extensive research has highlighted that fisheries stress can negatively affect reproduction by impairing individuals' ability to contribute to the increase in population abundance and neonates' survival and performance. Despite being one of the most threatened aquatic taxa, data on the reproductive consequences of fishing capture for Chondrichthyans are virtually non-existent, jeopardizing the assessment of the real consequences of this practice and the development of effective fisheries management measures. We investigated whether trawling in semi-captive conditions impairs the reproductive success of pregnant Trygonorrhina dumerilii, a viviparous ray commonly caught as bycatch in southern Australian recreational and commercial fisheries. To do this we collected data on the occurrence of stillborn neonates, parturition timing, and neonates' dimension at birth, growth rate and performance (boldness, reflex, swimming and burying ability). Results highlighted that neonates born from mothers subjected to trawling simulation not only have a significantly lower body mass at birth, as recorded in a previous experiment, but also have a different allocation of yolk reserves and a lower growth rate, respond differently in the burying test, and swim for shorter distances when a predator attack is simulated. Smaller size and lower growth rate might expose neonates to a higher rate of predation, and similarly, the altered burying and swimming behaviour may be associated with a lower ability to escape from a predator. Further investigation is needed, but these first data suggest a possible reduction in neonates' survival rate and parents' fitness that can ultimately have severe repercussions on recruitment and population abundance in affected species.

5838: The fossil record of modern sharks mainly consists of isolated teeth due to their poorly mineralized cartilaginous endoskeleton and a continuous tooth replacement that forms thousands of teeth during a sharks' lifetime. As a result, phylogenetic analyses of extinct shark taxa are mostly based on isolated teeth and therefore often lead to ambiguous results. The great white shark Carcharodon carcharias is known since the late Miocene, a period in which a number of big lamniform sharks occurred, i.e., †Otodus megalodon, †Cosmopolitodus hastalis and †Carcharodon hubbelli, which vanished after the Plio-Pleistocene marine megafauna extinction (2.5 mya). The evolutionary history of the great white shark remains highly debated and two hypotheses have been proposed: (1) C. carcharias is closely related to the megatoothed sharks, including †O. megalodon; (2) C. carcharias shares a more recent common ancestor with mako sharks and descended from the broad toothed mako shark †C. hastalis. Although the latter hypothesis is currently favoured, the occurrence of a narrow- and a broad-toothed form of †C. hastalis further complicates the reconstruction of the evolutionary history of the great white shark. Here we report of an exceptional find of two well preserved shark skeletons of a juvenile (TL ~1.7m) and an adult (TL ~5m) †Cosmopolitodus hastalis from the late Miocene Pisco Formation of Peru, which display broad teeth. The presence of articulated jaws allowed us to reconstruct the tooth files of this species and thus a more accurate phylogenetic analysis of lamniform sharks based on dental characters could be performed, including extinct mako sharks, Isurus spp. Furthermore, geometric morphometric analyses are performed to visualize the morphospace occupation of Isurus, †Cosmopolitodus and Carcharodon. This combined approach allowed us to reconstruct the origin of Carcharodon carcharias and the dental transition from fossil mako sharks to the extant great white shark.

5839: Sharks are the marine top predators responsible for regulating population of other tertiary and quarternary consumers (i.e. fishes, seals and dolphins) and maintaining a naturally balanced trophic chain in the marine ecosystem. However, there is limited understanding on how these marine top predators are ecologically and biologically adapted to consume and digest such a wide variety of prey items, without hampering functional traits of the gastro-intestinal tract. Gastro-intestinal microbial community of sharks plays important different biological roles including development of vertebrae in juveniles, metabolising a wide variety of complex biomolecules, nutrient absorption and immune system response. Hammerhead sharks are characterised by intraspecific ontogenetic and sex partitioning of resources (i.e. habitat and diet) as reflected by satellite tagging, genetics and stable isotope analyses. However, it's unknown how gut microbial biota changes between juvenile and adult sharks (ontogenetic partitioning of resources) and also between female and male individuals (sex partitioning of resources) within species. This study analysed gut microbial community structure and composition of two Sphyrna spp. based on 16S rRNA gene tag sequencing at both intraspecific and interspecific levels. DNA was extracted using Zymobiomics DNA miniprep kit and sequences generated using paired-end sequencing on the Illumina MiSeq platform following the manufacturer's instructions. Quantitative Insights into Microbial Ecology (QIIME) analyses revealed non-significant changes in microbial community structure between juvenile and adult individuals and also between sexes within each species. The core microbiota included Actinobacteria, Flavobacteria, Protobacteria and Firmicutes whereas Proteobacteria were the most abundant phylum. This suggests gut microbiome of hammerhead sharks may be shaped by broader biological factors such as the host genotype and ambient environmental conditions rather than diet.

5840: This study contributes to the abundance - biomass index, length-weight relationship (LWR) and bathymetric distribution of four deepwater elasmobranches (sharks) species obtained by the trawl fishing in the Antalya Bay (Eastern Mediterranean). The specimens of Centrophoridae (Centrophorus granulosus, Bloch & Schneider, 1801), Etmopteridae (Etmopterus spinax, Linnaeus, 1758), Scyliorhinidae (Galeus melastomus, Rafinesque, 1810) and Squalidae (Squalus blainvillei, Risso, 1827) were collected. As yet, a total of 25 specimens of C. granulosus, 586 specimens of E. spinax, 613 specimens of G. melastomus and 99 specimens of S. blainvillei were caught between the depths of 200-700 m. 5841: Our oceans are facing tremendous human-induced changes, including warming. As the temperature has increased, sudden warming events designated as marine heatwaves have become longer and more frequent with significant implications over marine ecosystems. As a crucial element of the marine environment, sharks may also be affected by these environmental changes. Exposure to ocean warming has shown to impact shark's predatory behavior, metabolism and overall fitness. However, the effects that a marine heatwave may have on these animals' physiology has not been addressed previously. Thus, the focus of our study was to investigate the impact of a marine heatwave (Δ3 °C) on the heamatological and respiratory systems of a juvenile temperate shark (Scyliorhinus canicula). To address this question, sharks were exposed to two treatments: control (18 °C) and category II marine heatwave (21 °C) for 15 days. We then analyzed the i) normal blood cell counts (e.g. erythrocytes, leucocytes and thrombocytes), ii) type and amount of EMNAs (erythrocyte nuclear morphological abnormalities), iii) spleen and heart to body ratios and iv) ventilation rates (before, initially and during the heatwave). According to our study, exposure to a category II marine heatwave drastically changed normal blood cell counts and ventilation rates. More specifically, the number of erythrocyte cells decreased, while the number of leukocyte and thrombocyte cells increased. Moreover, the amount of ventilation also increased. These findings may evidence that, during a sudden warming event, shark's ability to transport oxygen in red blood cells, linked to their need to ventilate more, might be significantly impaired. Furthermore, an increase of leukocytes and thrombocytes may explain the vulnerability and stress related to the increased temperature. As marine heatwaves are expected to aggravate with anthropogenic climate change, there is an urgency that should eager us to manage and mitigate its impacts.

5842: Monitoring trends in shark body size and weight is fundamental for understanding their life history traits and elucidating population dynamics. Traditionally, size and weight information is acquired through invasive techniques, involving capture and handling. These protocols may undermine conservation efforts by causing physical damage, behavioral alterations, premature birth and even the death of the captured animals. This study tested the effectiveness of laser photogrammetry as a non-invasive technique for measuring morphometrics from five shark species housed in aquariums. The measured morphometrics were examined in regression analyses to provide a comprehensive set of lineal relationships for the estimation of shark total length and weight. The results obtained indicate that (1) this approach is effort and cost-effective; (2) laser metrics are highly precise, which ensures the reliability of the gathered morphometric information; and (3) accurate total length and weight estimates can be obtained from short morphometrics. These insights indicate that laser photogrammetry is a useful technique for assessing growth and life history parameters from free-swimming sharks. Therefore, this technique may constitute a valuable tool for aquariums to monitor sharks' health status and determine food requirements and medication doses. Furthermore, it has the potential to provide useful insights when applied to monitor sharks in their natural environments in order to implement effective management strategies. The compiled also models ease the obtention of total length and weight data, providing a long-needed resource in shark monitoring programs.

5843: Sharks play both essential and diverse functional roles in marine ecosystems, having a remarkably long and successful evolutionary history. However, overfishing and habitat degradation, amidst other challenges, have ensued a steep population decline over the past decades. As CO2 emissions continue to increase, ocean acidification (OA) may come to pose an additional challenge to this group. In the present study, we investigated the potential impacts of OA-conditions (pCO2 ~900 µatm | Δ -0.3 pH units) over the embryonic development and juvenile metabolic physiology of a temperate shark, Scyliorhinus canicula. Aiming to evaluate the consequences of early exposure to high CO2 conditions, newly laid eggs were reared in either control or OA-treatment and, once hatched, individuals incubated under high CO2 were redistributed between both treatments. Both embryonic development, namely embryogenesis duration, hatching success, embryo activity, growth rate, body ratios, and juvenile metabolism, specifically their food intake, routine metabolic rate, maximum metabolic rate and aerobic scope, were evaluated. Overall, there were no significant changes in neither their development nor their metabolic physiology, regardless of early exposure to high CO2 levels. While this study highlights the coping capacity of sharks towards ocean acidification, the multiple and unpreceded pressures placed upon this group have the potential to undermine their inherent resilience. Hence, further research regarding different aspects of their biology and the numerous threats of the near-future is necessary to fully understand how this group may fare in the oceans of tomorrow.

5844: Serum biochemistry and hematology profile are used to assess the physiological status of animal individuals and populations. Therefore, establishing reference intervals for serum biochemical and hematological analytes for wild populations of marine keystone species is important for their conservation. However, no such intervals have been established to date for many species in the Eastern Mediterranean, including the dusky shark (Carcharhinus obscurus) and sandbar shark (Carcharhinus plumbeus). In the Mediterranean, C. obscurus and C. plumbeus are classed as data deficient and endangered species, respectively, according to the IUCN Red List. This study aims to establish reference intervals for serum biochemical and hematological analytes in these two species. Blood samples have been collected from wild dusky and sandbar sharks captured during the tagging seasons that Morris Kahn Marine Research Station has been conducting since 2016. In the winters of 2016 and 2017, blood samples were obtained from 14 C. obscurus and 7 C. plumbeus individuals. This ongoing study has and will further expand this database during the winters of 2018 and 2019. To this point, serum samples of 19 C. obscurus (18 females and one male) and 12 C. plumbeus (all males) individuals were analyzed by spectrophotometry using an autoanalyzer, including 15 analytes: urea, total proteins, total bilirubin, glucose, cholesterol, triglycerides, inorganic phosphorus, chloride, sodium, potassium, total calcium, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT), amylase, and creatine kinase (CK). For nine animals (four C. obscurus and five C. plumbeus), packed cell volume has been measured by centrifugation of heparinized capillaries, and manual leukocyte counts on blood smears have been done by microscopy. Preliminary results of serum biochemistry of both species are mostly consistent with findings of previous studies describing C. plumbeus in the Western Atlantic and other shark species in different locations. However, several analytes showed different values than previously described.

5845: Chondrichthyes (sharks, rays and chimaeras) are the most basal jawed vertebrate lineage possessing the basic features of the human innate and adaptive immune systems, and thus are a key taxon to understand the emergence and evolution of vertebrate adaptive immunity. However, the few studies conducted to date have not provided a clear picture of the complexity of the genes involved in adaptive immunity in this oldest extant vertebrate class. Our results show that for the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I genes, involved in antigen presentation to T cells and Nature Killer (NK) cells, there is indeed a very high diversity in genetic lineages and copy number variation across taxa, at least as complex as has been found in mammals. A new lineage of MHC-linked class I genes was found in all chondrichthyans, which appears to be single copy and likely monomorphic in Elasmobranchs but multicopy in Holocephalans. The predicted peptide-binding region is perfectly conserved in all Elasmobranchs tested, suggesting that the resulting protein(s) bind a unique set of peptides in all sharks and rays, rather than to allele-specific sets of peptides typical of the polymorphic classical class I molecules. Two previously reported yet poorly studied lineages of nonclassical MHC class I genes in cartilaginous fish were also examined but have only been found in sharks so far, although this may be due to a paucity of data for batoids and holocephalans. Our data clearly demonstrate that there was a division of labor among MHC class I lineages early in vertebrate evolution, with each lineage likely presenting different types of antigens to different subsets of T cells and/or NK cells.

5846: Elasmobranchs are among the marine species more threatened even by a moderate fishing intensity. Consequently, many elasmobranch species are now included in the red list of the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN). Effective management of endangered shark species requires a good understanding of their life histories traits. In this study, we estimated some growth and maturity parameters of two vulnerable shark species Mustelus mustelus (Linnaeus, 1758) and M. punctulatus (Risso, 1827) in the central Mediterranean Sea. The study is based on the analyses of vertebral growth bands; three different asymptotic growth models (e.g. VBGF, Logistic and Gompertz) have been applied with back-calculated length-at age data obtained using the Fraser-Lee equation. Results highlight that M. mustelus is a longer living species than M. punctulatus reaching also bigger sizes-at-ages. The growth parameters (sexes combined) of the two species were: L∞: 185 cm, K/year: 0.16 and t0: -3.2 (M. mustelus); and L∞: 105.5 cm and K/year: 0.27 with a t0:-1.4 (M. punctulatus). The growth curve of M. mustelus indicates an absolute annual growth rate of 15 cm by year during the first five years of life (i.e. between 35 and 105 cm TL). Maturity analysis show that M. punctulatus reaches the size at the onset of sexual maturity (L50%) at 94 cm TL (females) and 86.3 cm TL (males); M. mustelus matures at 105 cm (females) and 88 cm (males).

5847: The Norwegian skate Dipturus nidarosiensis (Storm, 1881) has only recently been recorded in the western and central Mediterranean Sea along the coast of Sardinia, off Algeria in Alboran Sea, in southern Adriatic and western Ionian Sea. An ancient presence of the Norwegian skate was hypothesised, despite its misclassification between D. nidarosiensis and other species from the same genus Dipturus. Infact its misclassification in the fishery data, mostly among the following species: D. oxyrinchus, D. batis, D. nidarosiensis and Rostroraja alba has not been uncommon since ancient times. These errors could have led to the underestimation of the risk of a dramatic decline and collapse of the spawning stock. Morevover, in the IUCN Red-List, the Norwegian skate is listed as near-threatened and it is considered rare in both the northeast Atlantic and the Mediterranean areas. Furthermore, due to its biological characteristics, which are similar to other elasmobranchs, such as low fecundity, slow growth and high length at first maturity, it is particularly vulnerable to environmental and anthropogenic pressures. From 2005 to 2019, the catches of Norwegian skate specimens were mostly repeated in two areas: the Sardinian Seas and Adriatic-Ionian area. In these two areas, a total of 64 specimens were caught and 10 morphological measurements and 6 meristic counts were taken on all captured specimens. The present study describes and characterizes, from a morphological point of view, the Norwegian skate specimens caught in the Sardinia Seas (Central Mediterranean Basin) and southern Adriatic-Ionian Sea (Central Mediterranean Basin). Morphological comparisons are made to provide further morphological keys for a correct classification of this species in the Mediterranean Basin. A multivariate approach analysis highlighted that some morphological features could be used to recognize two separated groups for the sampling areas (Sardinia; Adriatic-Ionian area), sex (male; female) and ontogenetic development (juveniles, adult).

5848: The Rajidae is a highly diverse family of elasmobranch fishes, including more than 285 species. Raja clavata is the most common and widespread skate in the N.E. Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea, and one of the dominant species in commercial landings. Currently, available data are either incomplete or incorrect due to the high level of morphological variability in rajids. Diversity of coloration patterns or polychromatism, has been reported previously for batoids (rajids, daysatids, potamotrygonids), which causes misidentification among closely related species. Therefore, morphological features are not always indicative of species relatedness. Additionally, several diagnostic characters distinctively visible in adults can be less evident in juveniles, making the taxonomy of younger specimens more difficult. In an attempt to minimize the gaps in our current knowledge on batoid biological traits, taxonomic issues were brought up in the Rajidae family. Specifically, taxonomic confusion had to be resolved among R. clavata, Raja polystigma and Raja montagui, which were caught in the eastern Ionian Sea. Our aim was to present an atlas of the polychromatism patterns of R.clavata, following the reliable identification of specimens using DNA sequencing. We applied DNA barcoding on 33 samples with taxonomic difficulties, and used the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit 1 (COI). We demonstrated that all 33 specimens were identified as R. clavata, confirming that the species exhibits high levels of polychromatism in the Ionian Sea like in Tunisia, Algeria and Marocco. Our findings show that accurate data from scientific surveys and landings are essential to assess conservation status and to develop suitable protection and management plans.

5849: In the past few years the knowledge on diseases and the disorders of elasmobranchs housed in public aquariums has increased, with particular reference to spinal deformities, thyroid pathologies, neoplasms, reproductive disorders and transmissible diseases (viral, bacterial mycotic and parasitic). Among these, bacterial infections mainly due to Vibrionaceae play an important role as often related to episodes of mortality in the presence of predisposing conditions. Vibrio harveyi (syn. V. carchariae) has been often associated with phenomena of meningitis or skin ulcers in different species of sharks. In the Aquarium of Cattolica (RN) over 100 elasmobranchs belonging to 16 different species are present. In the last few years, most of the occurred episodes of mortality in sharks were caused to bacteria, in particular V. harveyi. In detail, this pathogen has been identified as aetiological agent of disease outbreaks leading to the death of 4 young bonnethead shark (Sphyrna tiburo), 5 (4 juvenile and one adult) of black tip shark (Carcharhinus melanopterus), 3 juvenile bamboo shark (Chiloscyllium punctatum) and one adult nurse shark (Ginglymostoma cirratum). In these 2 last species also V. fischeri and Photobacterium damselae subsp. damselae were respectively isolated. In all cases meningitis and enteritis were observed. All episodes of mortality occurred during the quarantine period or after their transfer to a new tank. Therefore, opportunistic pathogens such as V. harveyi need to be considered relevant for the health of fish maintained in aquarium ecosystem and the application of effective management protocols can be useful to reduce the stress conditions to which the animals can be subjected especially during the phases following their transport and acclimatization to new habitat.

5850: Elasmobranchs are among the most threatened vertebrates on the planet, especially due to overfishing and habitat destruction. Despite this level of threat, the use of techniques to control their reproduction has been scarcely investigated as an approach to protect them in the wild or in captivity. Our main objective was to apply techniques commonly used in other fish species to achieve reproductive control in elasmobranchs. Four model species (Scyliorhinus canicula, Scyliorhinus stellaris, Galeus melastomus and Raja montagui) were the target with which to develop techniques that can be extrapolated to other species. Target species were obtained from fishing by-catch and from public aquaria. Urogenital and reproductive systems were anatomically described, and hepatosomatic and gonadosomatic indexes were calculated from by-catched species. Oocyte diameter was measured every month to establish their reproductive status through the year. Both in vivo and post-mortem extraction of sperm was achieved, by massage and gentle pressure near the urogenital pores or by catheterization with a urethral catheter. Spermatozoa were motile after activation with a Ringer solution adapted to elasmobranchs even when extracted from the seminal vesicle of dead fish stored at 4°C for 48 h. Sperm obtained from the cranial portion of the epididymis seemed to be immature and remained immotile in the 4 species, while it could be activated when was obtained from the caudal portion of the epididymis. Sperm volume and spermatozoa characteristics, such as size and number of helical gyres of the sperm head, size of midpiece and flagellum, and complexity and type of spermatozoa aggregates, were determined. Despite obvious sperm motility, large cell size (total length: 116-198 µm) made impossible its evaluation by standard CASA protocols. The techniques developed with our 4 target species were also tested in other specimens including a nurse shark (Gynglymosotoma cirratum) and a lesser devil ray (Mobula hypostoma).

5851: Sharks of the order Lamniformes comprise seven families with 15 extant species, including some of the most iconic shark species, like the great white shark (Carcharodon carcharias) and †Otodus megalodon. Lamniform sharks have a rich fossil record dating back to the Cretaceous with the oldest confirmed members of this group being known from the Barremian (125-130 mya). However, the origin of this group remains ambiguous, since sharks of the genus †Palaeocarcharias, small benthic sharks superficially resembling carpet sharks (Orectolobiformes) that are known from Middle Jurassic deposits (170 mya), are discussed to belong to this order. We used high resolution micro-CT scans obtained with the micro-CT scanner SkyScan 1173, to examine the tooth mineralization patterns of extant and fossil shark taxa and found three different tooth histologies: (1) orthodont teeth that have hollow pulp cavities surrounded by orthodentine, (2) osteodont teeth that have osteodentine and lack of orthodentine, (3) and pseudoosteodont teeth that have an osteodont core, which is surrounded by orthodentine. Our results show that exclusively osteodont teeth are only present in lamniform sharks and, therefore, suggest that this character represents a synapomorphic trait for this group. Additionally we could show that †Palaeocarcharias stromeri shares this unique tooth histology pattern with all lamniform sharks, suggesting that this shark indeed is the oldest known ancestor of this group.

5852: Data accumulated during a taxonomic study of Haematozoa of Rajidae (Elasmobranchs) have allowed a bioecological approach to the parasitism of the two most frequent, Trypanosoma rajae Laveran and Mesnil, 1902 and Haemogregarina sp Danilewsky, 1885 whose respective prevalences are: 15.06% and 9.58%. 8.2% of associations of the two parasites have been observed. The study was conducted on 113 rays belonging to four species of Rajidae (Raja asterias Delaroche, 1809 Raja miraletus Delaroche, 1809; Raja radula Linnaeus, 1758 and Raja undulata Lacepede, 1802) caught at two sampling sites on the Algiers coast: the port of Cap Djinet and the port of Bou Haroun. Statistical analysis of the data revealed a link between the age of the hosts and the parasitism. In the case of Trypanosoma rajae infestation, the oldest rays are the most infested, while in the case of infestation by Haemogregarina sp. host parasitism evolves in the same direction as age until a certain stage beyond which individuals defaunent of their parasites. An impact of parasitism on the health of the hosts was sought by the comparison of formulas leukocytes of parasitized and uninfected specimens; within the limits of the sample examined. The results do not allow any conclusion on any impact on the leucocyte composition of the infested hosts. The general parasitism observed in Cape Djinet (40.14%) seems more important than that of Bou Haroun (30.77%); the numbers treated, do not allow to conclude to a significant difference statistically.

5853: The spotted dogfish Scyliorhinus canicula is the common and widely distributed elasmobranch in the Northeast Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea. Recent studies have shown that this species has an important role in the trophic scheme of demersal fish communities, representing an important trophic link between invertebrates and larger predatory fish. It is also appreciated for the quality of its meat; this increases its commercial interest. Several studies suggest that this species is particularly susceptible to changes in environmental conditions, including temperature and oxygen availability, as well as exposure to pollutants. This can induce oxidative stress that in turn can lead to cellular damage and detrimental effects. Taking this into consideration, the evaluation of oxidative stress biomarkers assumes special importance, in an ecological, economical and public health perspective. However, to date no reference intervals for several oxidative biomarkers, have been reported for this shark. The aim of this study is to establish specific reference values for oxidative biomarkers in target tissues of S. canicula in order to assess the physiological status of the animal. Tissues samples (heart, muscle, gills, liver) have been collected from 32 spotted dogfish captured in the Mediterranean Sea (Follonica) during the period February-May 2018. Tissues were homogenized and subjected to spectrophotometric assays to asses the activity of SOD and LDH enzymes, markers of antioxidant activity and aerobic-anaeribic metabolism, as well as the levels of protein carbonylation and lipid peroxidation, indicative for oxidative stress damage. Preliminary results has been also analyzed in relation to tissue heavy metal accumulation.

5854: Atmospheric carbon dioxide has been increasing since the industrial revolution with a concomitant decrease in ocean pH, a phenomenon designated as ocean acidification (OA). OA may pose a threat to fundamental marine organisms, such as sharks. In this context, the current experiment aimed to test the effects of OA on different hematological parameters of the juvenile small-spotted catshark (Scyliorhinus canicula). Eggs were collected and randomly placed in either Control (pCO2 ~ 400 µatm) or High CO2 (pCO2 ~ 900 µatm, Δ -0.3 pH units) treatments, throughout the entire embryogenesis plus ~90 days after hatching. Hematological analysis was conducted on the number of normal blood cells (erythrocytes, leukocytes, and thrombocytes); presence of erythrocytes with nuclear abnormalities, and the erythrocyte cytoplasm to nucleus ratio was measured. Spleen and heart to body ratios were also evaluated. Overall, OA did not elicit significant differences in the studied parameters. Nonetheless, the decreasing trend in thrombocyte counts, which may have implications over clotting time, should foster further research. Although the present findings indicate that these sharks are possibly resilient to the prolonged OA exposure, future studies should scrutinize the scarcely recognized multi-stressors impacts (i.e. marine heatwaves, hypoxia, pollution, etc.) that sharks potentially will have to endure in the near future.

5855: The Greenland shark (Somniosus microcephalus) is the world's longest-lived vertebrate, with an estimated lifespan of 392±120 years. However, the mechanisms facilitating their extreme longevity remain unknown. Here, we generate the first de-novo transcriptome for the Greenland shark, as a tool to investigate the basic biology and ageing of elasmobranchs. Cardiac tissue from six Greenland sharks, between the approximate ages of 110 and 219 years, was collected from Bredefjord and Qaqortoq Fjords, Greenland, in the spring of 2017. A total of 236 million read pairs survived quality control, and were used to produce the transcriptome. The assembly process generated 149,000 transcripts with an N50 of 1,202bp, and a BUSCO score of 76.2%, making the transcriptome comparable in quality to that of other published squaliform elasmobranch transcriptomes. BLAST searching the transcripts against the whale shark (Rhincodon typus) genome identified 7,218 genes. Gene enrichment analysis revealed a significant over-representation of genes linked to mitochondrial function and ribonucleoprotein biogenesis, which is particularly interesting given that changes in mitochondrial quality are associated with many age-related diseases. A rank regression against total length, a proxy for age, identified 205 genes (205/7,218; 5x10-2 > p > 1x10-3, 0.99 > |r| > 0.88) displaying a significant correlation with length, including genes associated with antioxidant pathways, cardiomyocyte regeneration, and a dilated cardiomyopathy phenotype. This dataset is a valuable resource for future studies on the Greenland shark, particularly when investigating the molecular mechanisms underpinning age-related changes in the shark's physiology.

5856: The egg-cases can assume primary importance in the identification of the species they belong to, and provide a valid aid in the definition of the occurrence of the various species in different zones, as well as the exact definition of the deposition and nursery areas. In order to pick out the egg-cases' species with greater reliability, a dichotomous key for their specific identification has been set. This key mainly takes into account the morphological features of the egg-cases. A protocol for the standardized acquisition of morpho-biometric and meristic features is provided as pre-requisite for the most correct use of the identification key.

5857: Researches using stable isotopes analysis (SIA) of carbon (δ13C) and nitrogen (δ15N) in blood components (red blood cells and plasma) are still lacking, considering the challenge of sample collection in remote areas. There is poor information regarding the effect of tissue biochemical composition on isotopic ratios and there are few comparisons among different taxa in this regard. We explore the possibility that tissues biochemistry of different taxa affect isotopic results. During 2016 and 2017 we collected blood samples from shortfin mako sharks (Isurus oxyrinchus, n=70) and Guadalupe fur seals (Arctocephalus philippii townsendi, n=25). All the samples were centrifuged to obtain plasma in the case of mako sharks and serum for fur seals and then prepared for SIA. We did not find significant differences in δ15N values between the two species, but we found significant differences comparing δ13C in plasma of mako sharks (δ13C= -17.6 ± 0.9 ‰) and in serum of fur seals (δ13C= -20.3 ± 1.2‰). Furthermore, we tested the possible effect of different anticoagulants for sharks and lipids effect for Guadalupe fur seal samples. We did not find differences between species in both tests. The lack of significant differences in δ15N between the Guadalupe fur seal and the shortfin mako shark is likely related to their similar trophic level. The δ13C differences between the two species are probably due to serum and plasma biochemical characteristics, like lipid percentage in each species, more than differences in foraging area. These biochemistry characteristics in tissues are related to different adaptations in each taxon. This study shows the importance of developing more research on the influence of biochemistry features on isotopic results, because that blood component biochemistry may play a more important role in influencing isotopic signature than differences in foraging area.

5858: Skates (Rajidae) are oviparous Chondrichthyes which lay egg-cases on the sea floor, and while data of egg-cases' occurrence along the strandline exist, underwater field data helping to determine spawning grounds (presence of viable egg-cases) are very limited. During a demersal survey in Namibian waters in 2019, large quantities (5 to 21 kg) of ray egg cases were found at three locations. The egg cases were identified as belonging to the genus Rajella, possibly of the species Rajella barnardi or R. leopardus. These species were present together with the cases; confirmed by the trawl catch species identification. Two of the stations were located off the continental slope of Cape Cross not apart from each other, while the third one was located north off Cape Frio. The area can be described as confluence zone where warm tropical waters coming from the north meet subtropical colder waters flowing form the south creating a counter-clockwise water mass movement. The sites were at depths between 520 and 618 m. Over 90% of the cases were empty, the rest contained a yolk, which seemed to have been fertilized. Because the cases are made of collagen which breaks down very slowly, it is difficult to know when the older cases have been laid, but the empty ones were easily differentiable from the new-laid both by the texture and color. Although the species are not uncommon in these waters, the collection of such amounts of egg cases, both old and new, is an unusual observation pointing to a potential spawning area. This knowledge will help drawing a more detailed picture on the biology and distribution of the local species, which will contribute to improving their management.

5859: Over the past 30 years we have pioneered the use of archival and satellite tags to study the ecology, physiology and habitats of highly migratory tunas and lamnid sharks. Our research has provided large data sets on many species of endothermic fishes and sharks including the salmon, white and mako sharks, bluefin, and yellowfin tunas and billfishes. The value of having acquired these large data sets has given us a better understanding of their migrations, ecology, physiology, and behaviors of these animals in the wild. Combining these electronic tag data with fisheries data and genomics are key approaches for establishing life history, population biology, and protections for highly mobile predators in the open sea.

5860: In Israel, dusky and sandbar sharks (genus Carcharhinus) aggregate every winter at the warm water discharge of coastal power plants. This over wintering pattern is likely thermoregulatory in nature. Sightings of these species are increasingly rare in the Mediterranean, where shark populations have declined by 95% over the last decades. Sharks were tracked by acoustic telemetry, which enables detecting acoustic transmitters ('tags') by fixed underwater receivers. Since 2015, 17 sharks have been caught, measured and tagged in Hadera's hot waters, using acoustic tags and satellite tags. Acoustic tags are inserted into the shark's abdominal cavity, and satellite tags were attached to the dorsal fins. Both acoustic and satellite transmitters also recorded depth, and water temperature. Sharks were detected at the site for a long period (66 days ± 33.3 SD), and remained in the hot discharge while sea temperature kept decreasing. Daily movement analysis show sandbar sharks remain close to the bottom during daytime and moved to shallower water at night, while dusky sharks occupied very shallow water at all times. Data retrieved from one satellite tag showed a sandbar shark maintained the daily depth movement throughout its journey in open water. Temperature analysis show sharks stay within the elevated temperature zone throughout the season, away from the ambient temperature, until they leave the area completely. While one theory maintains that these aggregations are related to the gestation period in females, the residency of both female and male sharks suggest both genders benefit from the warm water. It is possible, that sharks are changing migration to warmer areas with the warm water at the station. Large scale movement study is crucial to understand the migration routes of these species in the Mediterranean Sea, and the implications of this phenomenon on their movement.

5861: The sandbar shark, Carcharhinus plumbeus is one of the biggest sharks inhabiting the Mediterranean. It is a cosmopolitan species and wellknown from Boncuk Cove in Mediterranean coast of Turkey. Primary nursery grounds, defined as areas where parturition occurs, of Boncuk Cove C. plumbeus population. The aim of study is to determine secondary reproduction and nursery area of sandbar shark from Yumurtalık Bight, Eastern Mediterranean Sea. On 24-27 July 2017, Sandbar shark specimens were accidentally caught at a depth of 7 to 9 m off the Yumurtalik Bight (36°44'44.39"N, 35°42'22.77"E) by a pelagic bluefish longline. A total of 8 specimens (4 females and 4 males) were transported to the laboratory on ice. Each fish was measured for total length to the nearest 0.1 cm, weight (W) was weighted to the nearest 0.1 g and sex was determined by the presence of claspers. Total lengths and weights of C. plumbeus specimens were 54.5-61.0 cm, 930 - 1484 g, for males and 49.6 - 62.4 cm, 918 - 1568 g, respectively for females. In shark species, the embryo is connected to the mother by an umbilical cord. The umbilical scars are still clearly visible on these newly born sharks. The open umbilical scar lengths were between 4.1 and 5.0 mm and they were used as an indicator. Thus, this study provides the records of neonate and juveniles sandbar shark from the Yumurtalik Bight. It was determined that Yumurtalik Bight can be the second reproduction and nursery area of the sandbar sharks in the Mediterranean after Boncuk Cove in Gokova Bay, Turkey.

5862: This study aims to provide general information regarding the effect of environmental factors on the occurrence of white sharks during ecotourism in Guadalupe Island, Mexico. The white sharks presence and environmental conditions were registered each hour during August-November of 2012-2014 in Rada Norte Bay (RNB). Analyzed environmental factors included sea surface temperature (SST), wind direction and speed, tide, moon phase, cloud cover, and water visibility. Sighting records were used to describe the white shark's probability of occurrence in relation to environmental factors, geographical position, and hour. Generalized additive models were applied using the presence/absence of the sharks as response variable according to the following categories: 1) Immature males; 2) Mature males; 3) Immature females; 4) Mature females. A total of 6,266 sightings of white sharks was registered according to sexual maturity during 98 days at RNB. Median from these records was 59 sightings per day (S.E.=5.96), and 9.82 sightings per hour (S.E.=1.22), with no significant differences in the sightings per hour related to the year (H2,90=6.35; P = 0.04), as confirmed by Bonferroni test. Regarding the month, a higher number of sightings per hour were observed during August (H3,90=21.20; P < 0.01), with no significant differences between the following months. The model for mature males suggests that there is a higher occurrence in the south part of RNB when SST is lower than 21°C, after new moon, and at any hour. In contrast, immature males' occurrence was higher in the west, during warm SST > 22°C, after full moon nights, and in the morning hours. Regarding females, mature individuals showed a higher probability of occurrence in the east, during warm SST > 23° C, early morning, and the last hours of the day. Explanations for these results will be discussed toward a potential segregation of white sharks in Guadalupe Island.

5863: Spatiotemporal variation of the deposition of skate's eggcases on beaches of the french metropolitan coast from 2005 to 2017 was studied. Due to the lack of knowledge on skates nowadays, we hypothesized that eggcases' distribution can provide additional informations for fishery surveys and spatio-temporal variations. Data were provided by a citizen science program involving 1900 volunteers. The proximal goal of this project was to evaluate the influence of environmental factors, detect a long term evolution and define massive strand areas. A methodological challenge consisted in performing a reliable analysis on a large dataset (~465000 eggcases, 1077sites) based on opportunistic data where absence or sampling effort were not notified. Fortunately, we were able to mobilize a second dataset (~240000 eggcases, 30sites) which is more standardized allowing to investigate temporal autocorrelation. Furthermore for spatial analysis, we established a 5 km buffer from the coast to collect all types of habitat around. Eggcases of seven species were encountered, mostly Raja undulata, R.clavata and R.brachyura. Adequate analysis performed on the two dataset provided the same results within and between year variations. The evolution of egg's deposition within a year shows a neat phenology with a peak of increase during winter followed by a decrease during summer. Eggcase's deposition from undulate rays tend to increase significantly (26%) throughout the years. However, for other species it didn't show any inter-annuals significant trends. Undulate's eggs were mostly found near littoral rocks and coarse sands and tend not to be present near deep habitats while thornback's eggs can be found near both deep and tidal zones. They are qualified as opportunistic for habitats and depth according to literature and experts. Blonde ray's eggs were found near shallow zones in rocks and sandy bottoms. These results suggest that egg's deposition of skates over time can allow us to have more information on the biology and ecology of species.

5864: Active acoustic surveys have been increasingly utilized as a non-extractive method for abundance estimation. These rely on species identification based on the focal animal's morphology, i.e., the dimensions of gas-filled structures such as the swim bladder, lungs, or other air cavities. Acoustic studies on elasmobranchs, which do not possess such structures, have dealt with the reflectivity of particularly large species or were unable to produce reliable size estimates, a prerequisite for density indexing. Furthermore, acoustic surveys typically employ narrow beam sonars which, with respect to highly-scattered populations, are mainly useful where animals are already known to occur as opposed to open-ocean waters. Thus, despite the potential usability of this method as the only non-extractive approach for real-time monitoring of deep-dwelling organisms, it remains limited to species of prominent acoustic features, as well as local-level surveys. We employed omni-directional transmitters to emit wideband acoustic signals and produce a time-delay image of continuously moving targets. The swimming trajectories of sharks and other species of apex predatory megafauna were compared with ground truth data to establish potential indicators to identify species irrespective of backscatter. Repetitions were performed in a variety of environmental settings throughout the Mediterranean marine space of Israel and included species that are listed as data deficient (DD), endangered (EN), and critically endangered (CR) in this region. Our findings provide for the non-extractive, fishery-independent sampling of highly-migratory megafauna across large spatial scales.

5865: An Ecopath mass-balance model was applied to explore the ecological role of demersal sharks and rays (SR) distributed in the Calabrian sector of the North-Western Ionian Sea (Central Mediterranean Sea). Biomass data (ton/km2y) mostly derived from the standardized biomass index of demersal species in the time series of the EU MEDITS trawl survey. Landings (ton/km2y) and Discards (ton/km2y) data of commercial species collected from the time series EU Data Collection Framework, together with Production, Consumption and Diet data, were used to model the food web in its stationary state. A total of 58 functional groups (FGs) described the Calabrian food web over the 3469 km2 from Punta Alice to Cape Spartivento between 10-800 m of depth. The demersal SR species aggregated in the FG of the Shelf SR benthic feeders, the Shelf SR benthopelagic feeders, the Bathyal SR benthic feeders, the Bathyal sharks benthopelagic feeders and the Blackmouth catshark Galeus melastomus. Trophic levels (TL), Omnivory Index (OI), Keystoness Index (KSI), Mixed Trophic Impacts (MTI) and Exploitation rate (E) were estimated to describe their ecological traits. The highest and lowest TL were estimated for the Bathyal SR benthic feeders (Cetrophorus granulosus, Dipturus oxyrinchus) (4.94) and Bathyal sharks benthopelagic feeders (Etmopterus spinax, Dalatias licha, Chimaera monstrosa) (4.26). The OI indicated the Bathyal sharks benthopelagic feeders as more generalist than the other groups. Within this FG the Etmopterus spinax and D. licha are the more abundant keystone predators. The highest E rates were estimated for the G. melastomus (0.65) and Dasyatis pastinaca, Mustelus mustelus, Raja asterias included in the Shelf SR benthic feeders (0.57). Trawl impacted with the highest negative values of MTI on the Shelf SR benthic feeders (-0.599), the Bathyal sharks benthopelagic feeders (-0.404), the Shelf SR benthopelagic feeders (Raja miraletus, Scyliorhinus canicula and S. stellaris) (-0.324) and G. melastomus (-0.154).

5866: A recent risk assessment for chondrichthyans (sharks, rays, and chimaeras) found some deepwater sharks were at relatively high risk of adverse impacts from fishing. Quantitative data for these species is limited, and some available information has been found to be unreliable. With a better understanding of spatial distributions, our knowledge of the risk to, and the status of these species would be more informed. This information would allow for the evaluation of potential stock boundaries, encourage comparisons of regional population structures, and overall, better inform fisheries management. Here, we investigate the suitability of several predictive modelling approaches, including vector-autoregressive spatio-temporal (VAST) models, to estimate spatio-temporal trends for seven deepwater sharks (Etmopterus granulosus, Centrophorus squamosus, Deania calcea, Centroselachus crepidater, Centroscymnus owstoni, Centroscymnus plunketi, and Dalatias licha) regularly caught in New Zealand deepwater trawl fisheries.

5867: The Western Central Atlantic (WCA) hosts a population of manta rays whose distribution and habitat preference is poorly understood to date. Obtaining this kind of information is crucial for effective conservation planning and implementation. In this study, we use ensemble ecological niche modelling (EENM) to predict the distribution of two sympatric manta ray species (Manta birostris and M. sp. cf birostris) in the WCA, and calculate the proportion of predicted suitable habitat that lies within protected areas. This technique has not been used to study the spatial ecology of manta rays at this scale before, but could prove to be a powerful tool in conservation planning. The EENM was developed combining 5,000 occurrence records derived from satellite tracking, diver observations, and verifiable social media posts. The predictions of the model indicate that suitable habitat for manta rays should be situated near the coast, in shallow and relatively warmer waters, especially near chlorophyll-α fronts. In the study region, key predicted suitable areas occur along the coasts of USA, Mexico, Nicaragua and Venezuela. Only 34% of predicted suitable habitat is encompassed by the present network of marine protected areas (MPAs), with just 0.2% in areas completely closed to fishing activities. The conservative life of oceanic manta rays makes this species sensitive to even moderate increases in mortality rates; for this reason, the existing MPAs may be likely to offer them little protection. As manta rays in the WCA are likely isolated from other populations worldwide, recolonization of the area following local extinction would be extremely unlikely and could even result in the loss of the endemic M. sp. cf birostris. Future conservation planning in the region should explicitly include conservation of manta rays in its targets, with particular focus on areas identified as key habitats for these species co-occurring in the WCA.

5868: A unique stronghold for the Critically Endangered Angelshark (Squatina squatina) is found in the Canary Islands, where the species is still frequently encountered by divers and fishers. This provides a great opportunity to conduct research into Angelshark ecology, as limited understanding of Angelshark habitat use, movement and site fidelity at is a major factor preventing effective species protection and conservation. A key focus for Angel Shark Project: Canary Islands (ASP:CI) (a collaborative initiative between Universidad de Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Zoological Research Museum Alexander Koenig and Zoological Society of London) is the investigation of juvenile Angelshark habitat in the region and identification of Angelshark nursery areas. The definition of shark nursery areas varies greatly in scientific literature, but ASP:CI have developed a multidisciplinary approach (using citizen science sightings, satellite imagery, focal surveys and mark-recapture techniques) to test the three nursery area criteria outlined in Heupel et al. 2007. Research over the last four years has identified that juvenile Angelsharks are present across a number of shallow, sheltered beaches in the Canary Islands. The team have identified two confirmed nursery areas, 13 potential nursery areas and 21 beaches where juvenile Angelsharks are observed. Mark-recapture work at the largest confirmed nursery area, Playa de Las Teresitas in Tenerife, confirms that juvenile Angelsharks remain present for up to 15 months. Data were used to develop a Guidance Document on the identification and protection of juvenile Angelshark habitat in the Canary Islands, which identifies eight key recommendations to improve protection of these areas.

5869: Labial cartilages are paired structures located outside the jaws whose purpose in sharks is not completely clear yet. Labial cartilages vary a lot in current shark species, ranging from three pairs to a complete reduction, from massive to slender and from long to short. In our current work we used CT-images as a non-invasive method to check for labial cartilages in different shark species occupying different ecological niches and using different feeding strategies. The goal is to find out if the labial cartilages are a phylogenetic or an ecological trait. Therefore, we used nine species, which then were grouped according to their ecological niche into deep living, oceanic and benthic. We were able to detect that the labial cartilages in the oceanic species – especially in those known for ram-feeding behavior – were massively reduced while the ones in the benthic species were well conserved and strongly developed. Among the species classified by us as deep living we saw rather unique adaptations in the labial cartilages in comparison to the benthic group. For example, the cookie-cutter shark Isistius brasiliensis has very strong, fused labial cartilages and the ones of the frilled shark Chlamydoselachus anguineus are very slender. Therefore, we assume that the labial cartilages are an ecological trait and can give additional information on the feeding behavior in sharks and are also capable of giving information about the feeding behavior in extinct species, since labial cartilages were also detected in fossils. In future works we are going to check on as many species as possible to either confirm or refuse this theory. A phylogenetic signal was not discovered so far and the developmental basis of these structures still is ambiguous.
